questions.q: According to this lesson's diagnostic checklist, what should you do first when a task fails?
options: Read the actual error in the log, since most failures name themselves
Immediately delete and rewrite the entire DAG
Restart the whole Airflow server without looking at anything
Assume it's always a code bug without checking further
questions.explain: The checklist starts with reading the real error in the log — most failures already tell you what went wrong before you investigate further.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say to check upstream task status before assuming the failing task itself is broken?
options: A task can fail because an upstream task never produced the file or row it expected, meaning the real bug is further back in the DAG
Upstream tasks are never relevant to a downstream failure
Checking upstream status is purely optional and rarely useful
Upstream tasks always succeed, so this step can be skipped
questions.explain: If an upstream task didn't produce expected output, the downstream task's failure is really an upstream problem, not a bug in the failing task itself.

questions.q: What does the real Admin > Connections screen shown in this lesson help diagnose?
options: Whether a task's error is caused by a missing or misconfigured connection ID, rather than a bug in the task's Python code
The CPU usage of the Airflow scheduler
The exact line number of a Python syntax error
How many DAGs exist in total across the deployment
questions.explain: A missing connection ID, or one pointing at the wrong host, is a real and common failure category the Connections screen surfaces directly.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what signal points to a code bug rather than an environment issue?
options: The failure reproduces identically every time, with the same input, in the same place
The task only fails in the production deployment, never locally
The failure started after a credential expired
The task fails on some runs but not others with identical inputs
questions.explain: A failure that reproduces consistently regardless of environment points to a genuine code bug that needs fixing in the DAG itself.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what commonly points to an environment issue rather than a code bug?
options: The DAG works locally but fails only in the deployed environment, with nothing in the DAG code having changed
The task fails with the exact same error on every machine it's ever run on
The DAG has never been executed anywhere before
The failure is a Python syntax error
questions.explain: Working locally but failing only in one deployment — with no code change — points to something external like a Connection, package, or permission difference.
